title: Pain relief in labour
blurb: Give accurate information on every option from breathing to epidural, and provide safe care and observations for each under NICE NG235.
question: Asha, 6 cm in her first labour at a freestanding midwifery unit, asks for an epidural. She wants to know whether it will slow her labour or lead to a caesarean. How should the midwife respond and what happens next?

teach.body: Formally: NICE NG235 section 1.6 asks professionals to reflect on how their own values shape their attitude to labour pain, to recognise that every woman's pain is unique (shaped by culture, socioeconomic status and neurodiversity), and to give accurate information and support her choice. In plain English: there is no 'right' amount of pain relief. The midwife explains each option honestly, including its benefits and side effects, and helps the woman get what she chooses.

teach.h: What to tell her about an epidural
teach.body: An epidural is available only in obstetric units, so transfer is needed from other settings. It gives more effective relief than opioids but may not always work fully. Complications during insertion can cause a severe headache. It is not associated with long-term backache, a longer first stage or more unplanned caesarean births, but it is associated with a longer second stage and more births with forceps or ventouse. It brings IV access and closer monitoring, so mobility may be reduced.

teach.h: Care of a woman with an epidural
items: Secure IV access first; no routine preload or maintenance fluids.
BP every 5 minutes for 15 minutes after establishing it and after each bolus of 10 mL or more.
Continuous CTG for at least 30 minutes after establishing it and after each 10 mL+ bolus.
Not pain-free 30 minutes after a dose: ask the anaesthetist to review.
Sensory block hourly; if not mobilising, straight leg raise hourly (cannot: anaesthetist).
Any comfortable position except lying flat on her back; continue through the third stage and repair.
After birth: straight leg raise by 4 hours after the last dose, or urgent anaesthetic review.

teach.h: Scenario: Asha asks for an epidural
teach.body: The midwife supports Asha's request and gives balanced information: it is the most effective relief, it will not lengthen her first stage or raise her chance of a caesarean, but it is linked with a longer second stage and more assisted births, and needs IV access and monitoring. Because epidurals are only available in obstetric units, she arranges an urgent transfer, contacting the ambulance service and coordinating midwife, and offers Entonox meanwhile. A midwife travels with her.

teach.text: Epidural myths: it does NOT lengthen the first stage, raise unplanned caesarean or cause long-term backache. It DOES lengthen the second stage and increase forceps or ventouse births. And no pool within 2 hours of an opioid.

items: Latent labour: breathing, bath or shower, massage; do not offer aromatherapy, yoga or acupressure.
Pool: water up to 37.5°C, check hourly; not within 2 hours of opioids.
Sterile water injections for back pain: 4 points, relief from 10 min to 3 h.
Entonox: nausea, light-headedness. Opioids: limited relief, give an antiemetic; neonatal effects.
Epidural: obstetric unit; longer second stage and more instrumental births.
Epidural care: BP 5-minutely for 15 min, CTG 30 min, block hourly, review if not pain-free at 30 min.

summary: You can now explain every pain relief option in NICE NG235, including where it is available and its effects on the woman and baby. You can also provide safe care for women using water, opioids and epidurals, including the observations and escalation points.

A.q: Mo has been given intramuscular pethidine in labour. What should the midwife also give?
A.why: NG235 1.6.19: if an intravenous or intramuscular opioid is used, also administer an antiemetic.

whyNot.0: IV fluids are not routinely needed with an opioid.
whyNot.2: Routine maternal oxygen is not indicated.
whyNot.3: Naloxone is a treatment for opioid toxicity, not given in advance.

A.q: What is the maximum recommended temperature of the water for a woman labouring in a birth pool?
A.why: NG235 1.6.11: the water temperature should not be above 37.5°C; monitor the woman's and the water's temperature hourly.

whyNot.0: 38.5°C is too hot and risks maternal pyrexia.
whyNot.2: 39.0°C is far above the recommended maximum.

A.q: For which problem should sterile water injections be considered in labour?
A.why: NG235 1.6.14: consider intracutaneous or subcutaneous sterile water injections for women in labour with back pain.

whyNot.0: They are not used for postnatal perineal pain.
whyNot.1: They are recommended for back pain specifically.

B.q: Freya asks how an epidural might affect her labour. Which information is accurate?
options: More instrumental births and a longer second stage
A longer first stage of labour for most women
A higher chance of an unplanned caesarean birth
Long-term backache after the baby is born
B.why: NG235 1.6.26: an epidural is associated with a longer second stage and an increased chance of forceps or ventouse birth.

whyNot.1: Epidural is not associated with a longer first stage.
whyNot.2: Epidural is not associated with more unplanned caesarean births.
whyNot.3: Epidural is not associated with long-term backache.

B.q: Kerry had intramuscular diamorphine an hour ago and now wants to get into the birth pool. She is alert. What should the midwife advise?
options: She can get into the pool now
Wait until 2 hours after the dose
No pool for the rest of labour
B.why: NG235 1.6.20: women should not enter water within 2 hours of opioid administration, or if they feel drowsy.

whyNot.0: Entering water within 2 hours of an opioid is not advised.
whyNot.3: She can use the pool once 2 hours have passed and she is not drowsy.

B.q: An epidural is being established for Lina. How often should her blood pressure be measured?
B.why: NG235 1.6.30: during establishment, and after boluses of 10 mL or more, measure BP every 5 minutes for 15 minutes.

whyNot.0: This is not frequent enough during establishment.
whyNot.2: This is not the NG235 schedule during establishment.
whyNot.3: Hourly checks are for the sensory block, not BP during establishment.

C.q: Thirty minutes after an epidural top-up, Maya is still in significant pain. What should the midwife do?
C.why: NG235 1.6.30: if the woman is not pain-free 30 minutes after each administration of local anaesthetic or opioid solution, ask the anaesthetist to review.

whyNot.0: The 30-minute rule requires anaesthetic review, not repeated dosing by the midwife.
whyNot.1: Waiting longer leaves her in pain and delays review.
whyNot.2: Adding an opioid does not address a poorly working epidural.

C.q: Asha, 6 cm at a freestanding midwifery unit, asks for an epidural. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Explain transfer is needed and arrange it
Arrange for an epidural to be sited at the unit
Start remifentanil PCA at the midwifery unit
Lend her an NHS TENS machine to use instead
C.why: Epidural analgesia is available only in obstetric units, so transfer is needed (NG235 1.6.26); urgent transfer for pain relief is category 2 (1.5.4).

whyNot.1: Epidurals are not available in midwifery units.
whyNot.2: Remifentanil PCA is used only in obstetric units (1.6.22).
whyNot.3: TENS devices are not provided by the NHS.

C.q: Four hours after the last epidural dose following birth, Lucy cannot do a straight leg raise. What should the midwife do?
options: Reassess her leg strength in another 4 hours
Help her to walk to the toilet to void
Remove the epidural catheter and observe her
C.why: NG235 1.12.2: check that women can perform a straight leg raise by 4 hours after the last anaesthetic dose; if not, contact the obstetric anaesthetist for urgent review.

whyNot.0: Persistent weakness at 4 hours needs urgent review now.
whyNot.1: Walking with leg weakness risks falls and delays review.
whyNot.3: This does not address the possible complication causing weakness.

reteach.title: A ladder she can climb or not
reteach.question: Picture pain relief as a ladder from breathing to epidural. Who chooses the rung, and what comes with each step up?

blocks.body: Lower rungs (breathing, water, massage, sterile water injections) are available almost anywhere with few side effects. Entonox and opioids are in every setting but bring nausea or drowsiness, and opioids can affect the baby. The top rung, epidural, is the most effective but means an obstetric unit, IV access, more monitoring and a longer second stage. She chooses; the midwife informs.

blocks.text: Epidural: the first stage is not longer; the second stage is.

explain.body: Advise that breathing exercises, a shower or bath, and massage may reduce pain in latent labour. Do not offer aromatherapy, yoga or acupressure in latent labour, or acupuncture, acupressure or hypnosis in labour, but support a woman who chooses them.

test.q: Which options does NICE NG235 advise may reduce pain in the latent first stage?
options: Breathing, bath or shower, and massage
test.why: NG235 1.6.3: advise that breathing exercises, a shower or bath, and massage may reduce pain in the latent first stage.

whyNot.0: Do not offer aromatherapy or yoga for latent labour (1.6.4).
whyNot.2: Do not offer acupressure or hypnosis (1.6.4, 1.6.8).
whyNot.3: Acupuncture is not offered and TENS is not provided by the NHS.

explain.body: A 50:50 mixture of oxygen and nitrous oxide, available in all birth settings. It may reduce pain, but may make her feel nauseous and light-headed.

test.q: Which side effects of Entonox should the midwife explain?
test.why: NG235 1.6.17: Entonox may make her feel nauseous and light-headed.

whyNot.0: Neonatal respiratory depression is a side effect of opioids.
whyNot.1: Long-term backache is not linked to Entonox (or epidural).
whyNot.2: Leg heaviness is linked to regional analgesia.

explain.body: Pethidine, diamorphine and other opioids provide limited relief and can cause maternal drowsiness, nausea and vomiting, and short-term respiratory depression and drowsiness in the baby that may last several days and make breastfeeding harder.

test.q: Which effect on the baby should be explained before opioid analgesia in labour?
options: Jaundice within the first 24 hours of life
Low blood glucose for the first day
Hip instability found at the newborn check
test.why: NG235 1.6.18: opioids may cause short-term respiratory depression and drowsiness in the baby, which may last several days and make breastfeeding more difficult.

whyNot.1: Early jaundice is not a listed opioid effect.
whyNot.2: Hypoglycaemia is not a listed opioid effect.
whyNot.3: Hip instability is unrelated to analgesia.

explain.body: Perform continuous CTG for at least 30 minutes during establishment of regional analgesia and after each further bolus of 10 mL or more.

items.label: CTG after establishing or 10 mL+ bolus

test.q: For how long should continuous CTG be performed after an epidural is established or after a bolus of 10 mL or more?
test.why: NG235 1.6.36: continuous CTG for at least 30 minutes during establishment and after each further bolus of 10 mL or more.

whyNot.0: 10 minutes is shorter than NG235 requires.
whyNot.1: NG235 sets a minimum of 30, not 60, minutes.
whyNot.3: 5 minutes is far shorter than recommended.
